newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Shorter-dated yen calls remain red hot.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Shorter-dated yen calls remain red hot.

text.p: Yen calls in dollar/yen options, particularly the gamma-rich shorter dates, remained aggressively bid as the dollar plumbed lows and edged closer to a psychological barrier of 110 yen, U.S. traders said.
End-user hedging interest kept drizzling in, while market-makers were passing on negative gamma positions in the downside strikes to the market like hot potatoes, they said.
"It's just feeding on itself," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist I.D.E.A. Inc, adding that the dollar's rapid decline was not giving the market time to absorb the surge in demand for yen calls.
"If there's any hesitation about squaring any negative 'wing' (out-of-the-money) gamma, you're sitting on top of those strikes," he said.

Higher gamma provides quicker price acceleration against spot movement. When spot gaps toward the strike price of a low-delta option, gamma itself picks up quickly, making negative exposures extremely painful.

With spot making only mild recovery from an early low of 110.62 yen, a near-term test of 110 yen looked like a distinct possibility, traders said, adding that there was talk about big exotic option barrier prices between 109 and 110 yen.

"I think the market is afraid that we will make a push for those barriers and we haven't seen the bottom in dollar/yen yet," said Soma Rao, first vice president and options sales manager of Smith Barney in New York.
One-month dollar/yen implied volatility stood at 14.5/14.8 percent at U.S. midsession, up nearly a full point from late Tuesday levels. One-year was up about 0.4 point to 11.5/11.7.
Risk-reversal, the cost of swapping equally out-of-the-money puts and calls, for one-month 25-delta options remained at around 2.0 points in favor of yen calls after trading as high as 2.5 earlier.
While most traders saw yen calls as extremely rich, there was little interest to go against the grain.

"Even if it's 2.5 vols in risk reversal, the market is justified in paying that kind of levels, not from the absolute moves (actual volatility) but on a mark-to-market basis," Rao said, noting that market-makers had to contain risk parameters to certain levels. "Even if you could argue that 110 is going to be the bottom, you still have a mark-to-market loss of significant proportion (when spot is at 110)."
He said one-month volatility at 16 or 17 percent was possible if spot sank below 110 yen.
Dollar/mark volatilities also firmed but to a much lesser extent as spot stayed in familiar ranges above 1.71 marks.
"Even though it's been volatile, it's basically been going back and forth in a range," Rao said.

Choppy trading inside the ranges, however, has kept the volatility curve flat as it justified holding gamma while dampening interest in paying too much vega, traders said. Various meetings of top European officials and the Group of Seven summit in the coming weeks also supported the front end.
One-month dollar/mark stood at 9.6/9.9 percent, up about 0.2 point on the day, while one-year gained 0.15 to 9.55/9.75.
